name: Angular velocity
seoDesc: Angular velocity: work out time (t) from the initial angle and the angle change. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: time (t) is what the Angular velocity calculator works out, and it gets there from the initial angle, the angle change, the angular velocity (ω) and the velocity. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Angular velocity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Angular velocity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports time (t) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the initial angle (α₁), the angle change (Δα), the angular velocity (ω) (Method 1: Angle difference) and the velocity (v).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show initial and final angles”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in degrees. The unit chip switches it to any of the 12 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in radians per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters per second. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Angular velocity calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Time (t)=angle change (Δα) ÷ angular velocity (ω)
Angular velocity (ω)=velocity (v) ÷ radius (r)
Final angle (α₂)=initial angle (α₁) + angle change (Δα)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in radians per second, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.
  • Shown in degrees, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Rotational speed, opening in radians per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Rotational speed, opening in radians per second

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Angular velocity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the initial angle, the angle change and the angular velocity (ω) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Angular velocity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns time (t), derived from the initial angle, the angle change and the angular velocity (ω). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Angular velocity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the initial angle, the angle change, the angular velocity (ω) and the velocity, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter initial angle (α₁) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Initial angle (α₁) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Angular velocity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
